questions.question: How do you read a Java stack trace to find the source of an error?
questions.title: How to Read a Java Stack Trace
questions.direct_answer: Read the exception type and message, then inspect its cause and suppressed-exception sections. Frames are listed from the most recent captured call toward older callers. Start with the top relevant frame in application code, but treat it as evidence rather than proof of the bug; also inspect values, configuration, and the cause chain.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Read throwable type and message before the frames
- Frames run from the most recent captured call toward older callers
- Follow `Caused by:` and inspect `Suppressed:` sections
- Start with a relevant application frame, not blindly the first one
- Use the matching deployed source revision and runtime context

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I read a Java stack trace in layers. First I read the throwable type and message. Then I check whether the trace contains `Caused by:` or `Suppressed:` sections, because the outer exception may only describe the failed operation. The `at` frames run from the most recent captured call toward older callers. I locate the nearest relevant frame in application code and open the source revision that produced the deployed bytecode. That frame is a starting point, not automatic proof of fault: the application may have passed bad data into a library, configuration may be wrong, or the dependency itself may fail. For example, an outer `OrderLoadException` can lead to a caused-by `SQLException`, while `OrderRepository.find` shows which application operation triggered it. I combine the chain, inputs, versions, and surrounding logs before changing code.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
A Java stack trace starts with a throwable type and message. Each following `at` line is a captured stack frame: class, method, source file, and line when debug information is available. The first frame is the most recent captured call and is often where the throwable was created or raised.

Wrapped failures appear under `Caused by:` and cleanup failures may appear under `Suppressed:`. Read the outer message for operation context and then follow causes until the low-level failure relevant to the investigation. The deepest cause is not automatically the most useful explanation.

Find the first frame in code the team owns near that failure, open the exact revision that produced the trace, and inspect inputs and surrounding state. An application frame may have passed invalid data to a correct library, while a framework or dependency can also contain the defect.

sections.title: Reading Order
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[Throwable type and message] --> B{Cause or suppressed failure?}
    B -->|Cause| C[Read outer context and lower-level cause]
    B -->|No| D[Inspect most recent frames]
    C --> D
    D --> E[Find nearest relevant owned frame]
    E --> F[Check source revision, inputs, and configuration]
```

sections.title: Anatomy of a Trace
sections.content:
```text
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke
    "String.length()" because "name" is null          <-- (1) WHAT
    at com.app.UserService.greet(UserService.java:25)   <-- (2) WHERE it was thrown (your code)
    at com.app.UserController.hello(UserController.java:14) <-- (3) caller (your code)
    at org.springframework.web...invoke(...)            <-- (4) framework, ignore for now
```

Read it as: a NullPointerException (1) was thrown at `UserService.java:25` (2), which was called from `UserController.java:14` (3). Start at line 25.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reading only the last frame**: frames run from the most recent call toward older callers.
- **Ignoring outer context**: the deepest cause may not name the failed business operation.
- **Blaming the first application frame**: it is an investigation point, not proof.
- **Ignoring suppressed exceptions**: resource cleanup can add a second useful failure.
- **Opening the wrong source version**: line numbers must match the deployed build.

questions.question: What does 'Caused by' in a Java stack trace mean and how do you use it?
questions.title: Caused By — Nested Exceptions in Java Stack Traces
questions.direct_answer: `Caused by:` shows that one throwable wraps another as its cause. Java prints the outer failure first and then the cause chain, which preserves both higher-level operation context and lower-level detail. The last cause is the deepest recorded cause, but diagnosis should use the full chain rather than assuming the last message alone is the root problem.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `Caused by:` is a wrapped throwable stored as the cause
- Outer exceptions add operation or domain context
- Deeper causes preserve lower-level detail and original frames
- The deepest recorded cause is not automatically the actionable defect
- `Suppressed:` exceptions are separate from the cause chain

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: `Caused by:` means a throwable has wrapped another throwable as its cause. A repository might catch `SQLException` and throw `OrderLoadException("Could not load order 42", sqlException)`. The outer exception says which operation failed, while the cause keeps the database type, message, and frames. Java prints the wrapper first and then each cause, sometimes abbreviating shared frames with `... n more`. I follow the whole chain. The last cause is the deepest recorded failure, but it is not automatically the code change to make: a connection refusal may come from wrong configuration, and a parsing failure may come from invalid input supplied higher up. I also check `Suppressed:` blocks separately because try-with-resources can preserve a close failure there.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Java exceptions can retain another throwable in their `cause` field. A repository may catch `SQLException` and throw `DataAccessException("Could not load order 42", cause)`. The outer exception explains the failed operation; the cause preserves the database detail and frames.

The printed trace nests each cause under `Caused by:` and may abbreviate shared frames with `... n more`. Follow the chain without losing the outer messages. The deepest cause is the lowest recorded failure, but the actionable defect may be invalid application input, configuration, or a bad retry higher in the chain.

`Suppressed:` is different. Try-with-resources can preserve a close failure as suppressed while another exception remains primary. Check both structures during a complex resource failure.

sections.title: Following the Chain
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[OrderLoadException
operation context] -->|Caused by| B[DataAccessException
persistence context] B -->|Caused by| C[SQLException
lowest recorded failure] A --> D[Use the full chain to find the actionable cause] C --> D ```

sections.title: Swallowing the Cause — Chain Lost
Wrapping with the Cause — Chain Preserved
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reading only the wrapper**: it may omit the low-level detail.
- **Reading only the deepest cause**: it may omit the operation and input context.
- **Dropping the cause**: `new Wrapper(message)` loses the original frames.
- **Wrapping without new context**: repeated generic wrappers add noise.
- **Confusing `Suppressed:` with `Caused by:`**: they represent different relationships.

questions.question: How do you read a NullPointerException stack trace in Java?
questions.title: Reading a NullPointerException Stack Trace
questions.direct_answer: Read the NPE message and top frame to locate the failed dereference. Modern JVMs can describe which expression was null, but the wording and availability depend on the runtime and bytecode. The line locates the symptom; trace how the null value entered that path instead of adding a blind null check.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Message plus top frame locate the failing dereference
- Modern JVMs may identify the null expression in detail
- Use the source revision that produced the bytecode
- The trace line shows the symptom, not why the value became null
- Fix the null contract or initialization; do not add a blind check

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For a NullPointerException, I read the message and top frame to locate the failed null-sensitive operation. Modern JVMs can provide a helpful message such as `Cannot invoke "String.length()" because "name" is null`, though the exact detail depends on the runtime and expression. I open the source revision that matches the build, then trace the value backward. It may come from a missing map key, an unexpected repository result, failed injection, or partially initialized state. The line where the program crashed is the symptom; the contract that allowed null is often the cause. For example, if `users.get(id)` may return null, the code should define absence—perhaps return `Optional`, throw a domain not-found exception, or handle it—not simply add a check that hides the error.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
A NullPointerException trace identifies the method and source line where a null-sensitive operation failed. Modern Java runtimes can produce helpful messages such as `Cannot invoke ... because ... is null`, giving more expression detail than older generic messages.

That detail is diagnostic, not a stable program API. Optimized or complex expressions and different runtime settings may provide less information. Open the exact deployed source line and separate chained calls into their intermediate values if the null source is unclear.

Then trace the value backward: was an input contract violated, did a repository return null instead of `Optional.empty()`, did dependency injection fail, or was state published before initialization? Fix the contract or initialization point. A defensive null check is correct only when absence is a valid case with defined behavior.

sections.title: From NPE to Root
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[NPE first line
which var is null] --> B[Top 'at' line
file:line of dereference] B --> C[What assigned that variable?] C --> D{Source of null} D --> E[Map/get returned null] D --> F[Field never initialized] D --> G[Method returned null] ```

sections.title: The Bug — Unguarded Null
The Fix — Guard or Optional
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Ignoring the helpful message**: on Java 14+ it literally names the null variable — read it.
- **Fixing the symptom**: adding a null check at the crash site without asking why it was null upstream.
- **Confusing reference vs object**: the *variable* is null, not the method you called on it.

questions.question: How do you identify your own code versus framework code in a Java stack trace?
questions.title: Identifying Your Code vs Framework Code in a Stack Trace
questions.direct_answer: In a stack trace, **your code's `at` lines start with your project's package** (e.g. `com.myapp...`), while **framework lines start with `org.springframework`, `java.`, `jakarta.`, `org.hibernate`, etc.** The bug is almost always in **your** lines, so scan the trace and focus on the topmost frame in your own package — the framework frames above it are just the plumbing that called you.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Package names distinguish application, JDK, framework, and library frames
- Start near the relevant exception or cause, then find the nearest owned frame
- An owned frame is an investigation point, not proof of fault
- Configuration and input can make a framework frame fail
- Library defects remain possible; use versions and evidence

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I separate frames by their fully qualified package names. A frame such as `com.example.orders.OrderService.place` belongs to the application, while `java.`, `jdk.`, `org.springframework`, and dependency prefixes identify other layers. Starting at the relevant throwable or cause, I find the nearest application frame because it shows how owned code reached the failure. I do not assume that line contains the bug. It may have passed an invalid value to correct framework code, a property may be configured incorrectly, or a library may genuinely contain a defect. For example, a Hibernate frame followed by `OrderRepository.findCustom` tells me to inspect both the repository query and the database error. Package recognition narrows the search; the message, cause chain, versions, and runtime data decide the diagnosis.

sections.title: Following a stack trace back into application code
sections.content:
A frame's fully qualified class name shows its package. Application frames may begin with `com.example.orders`, while Java and framework frames may begin with `java.`, `jdk.`, `org.springframework`, or another dependency package.

Start from the relevant throwable or cause and locate the nearest frame in code the team owns. For example, `OrderService.place(OrderService.java:42)` below MVC frames is a useful inspection point because it connects the failure to application behavior.

Package ownership does not decide fault. Application code can pass an invalid value into a correct framework, configuration can make a framework fail, and a library can contain a bug. Combine frames with the exception message, cause chain, versions, and runtime inputs.

sections.title: Telling Frames Apart
sections.content:
emerald|Your code|~Start debugging here|com.myapp.*|your package prefix|topmost = focus
blue|Framework|~Just plumbing|org.springframework.*|org.hibernate.*|usually not the bug
amber|JDK|~Standard library|java.* / jakarta.*|rarely your bug|skip past
rose|Tip|~IDE folds these|collapse library frames|jump to your line|less noise

sections.title: Spotting Your Frame
sections.content:
```text
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: id must be positive
    at java.base/java.util.Objects.checkIndex(...)         <- JDK (skip)
    at org.springframework.web...invokeHandlerMethod(...)  <- framework (skip)
    at com.myapp.order.OrderService.find(OrderService.java:31)  <- YOUR code: START HERE
    at com.myapp.order.OrderController.get(OrderController.java:18) <- your caller
    at org.springframework.web...doDispatch(...)           <- framework (skip)
```

The two `com.myapp` lines are yours; everything else is the framework calling into (and out of) your handler.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Blaming the framework name at the top** without checking the caller and input.
- **Blaming application code automatically** when a dependency or runtime version may be faulty.
- **Ignoring the cause chain** and examining an unrelated outer frame.
- **Using a package rule only** instead of reading messages and configuration.
- **Opening a different source revision** from the deployed build.

questions.question: What does a StackOverflowError stack trace look like and what causes it?
questions.title: StackOverflowError — What It Looks Like and Why It Happens
questions.direct_answer: `StackOverflowError` means one thread exhausted its Java call stack. Repeated frames usually reveal direct or mutual recursion with no reachable stop, but very deep legitimate call chains or unusually large frames can also exhaust the stack. Find the repeating cycle and input, fix the termination/progress rule or use an iterative design where appropriate; do not merely increase stack size before understanding the cause.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- The current thread exhausted its call-stack space
- Repeated frames often reveal direct or mutual recursion
- Finite but very deep calls can also overflow
- Verify progress toward a reachable base case
- Prefer an iterative design when input depth is unbounded; tune `-Xss` only with evidence

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: `StackOverflowError` means the current thread could not allocate another Java stack frame. A repeated method or short cycle in the trace usually reveals direct or mutual recursion that is not making progress toward a base case. For example, a tree walk can work on balanced data but overflow on a highly skewed tree with unbounded depth. I find the shortest repeated frame cycle and the input that causes it, then check both termination and progress. Infinite recursion is common, but a finite and extremely deep call chain or large frames can also exhaust the stack. Where input depth is not safely bounded, an explicit heap-based stack or iterative algorithm is often better. Raising `-Xss` only moves the limit and can reduce the number of threads the process can support, so it is not the first fix.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Every Java method call consumes a stack frame on the current thread. When the thread cannot allocate another frame, the JVM throws `StackOverflowError`.

A trace often repeats one method for direct recursion or a small group for mutual recursion: `a → b → a`. Locate the shortest repeated cycle and the input that fails to make progress toward its base case. Recursion that works for small trees can still overflow on a highly skewed or attacker-controlled structure.

Not every overflow is an infinite loop. A finite but very deep graph traversal, recursive parser, generated proxy path, or large per-frame state may be enough. An iterative algorithm with an explicit heap-based stack can remove call-stack depth when appropriate. Raising `-Xss` only changes the limit and can reduce how many threads fit in memory, so measure it after correcting the design.

sections.title: Why the Stack Overflows
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[method calls itself] --> B{base case reached?} B -->|No / never| C[push another stack frame] C --> A B -->|Yes| D[returns - stack unwinds] C --> E[stack space exhausted
StackOverflowError] ```

sections.title: The Bug — Missing/Wrong Base Case
The Fix — Reachable Base Case (or Iterate)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **No base case** (or one that's unreachable, e.g. `n != 0` with a step that skips 0).
- **Mutual recursion**: `a()` calls `b()` which calls `a()` with no termination.
- **Accidental recursion**: a getter calling itself, or `toString()`/`equals()` referencing themselves.

questions.question: What is a chained exception (exception cause) in a Java stack trace?
questions.title: Chained Exceptions in Stack Traces
questions.direct_answer: A chained exception keeps a lower-level throwable as the `cause` of a higher-level exception, usually with `new HigherLevelException(message, cause)`. This lets the outer layer add useful context without losing the original type, message, and frames. Read the complete chain; the deepest recorded cause is not always the most actionable explanation.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- A wrapper retains another throwable through its `cause`
- The outer message adds operation or domain context
- Passing the cause preserves its type, frames, and nested causes
- Avoid wrappers that add no useful context
- Suppressed cleanup failures are not the same as causes

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A chained exception is a higher-level throwable that keeps a lower-level throwable in its `cause`. For example, `new OrderLoadException("Cannot load order 42", sqlException)` adds useful operation context without losing the SQL exception's type, message, and frames. The printed trace shows the wrapper first and then `Caused by:` blocks. I read the full chain: the outer layers explain what the system was doing, while the deeper cause explains the lowest recorded failure. The deepest cause is not automatically the actionable defect; incorrect input or configuration may have produced it. A good wrapper adds context and passes the original cause. Re-wrapping at every layer with a generic message only adds noise. `Suppressed:` exceptions, often from resource cleanup, are related diagnostics but are not links in the cause chain.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Exception chaining preserves two kinds of information. The outer exception names the operation or domain failure, while its cause retains the lower-level technical failure.

For example, `OrderLoadException("Cannot load order 42", sqlException)` tells the caller what operation failed and lets diagnostics inspect the database exception. Passing only `sqlException.getMessage()` would discard its type, cause chain, and stack frames.

A useful wrapper adds context and preserves the cause. Avoid wrapping at every layer with no new information. Also distinguish causes from suppressed exceptions, which commonly record secondary failures during resource cleanup.

sections.title: The Cause Chain
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[OrderLoadException
which operation failed] -->|cause| B[DataAccessException
which boundary failed] B -->|cause| C[SQLException
lowest recorded failure] A --> D[Diagnosis uses context plus cause] C --> D ```

sections.title: Losing the Cause
Preserving the Cause
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Discarding the cause** when creating a wrapper.
- **Adding a wrapper with no useful context** at every layer.
- **Assuming the deepest cause alone names the fix**.
- **Exposing low-level exceptions directly** across an API boundary without translation.
- **Ignoring suppressed cleanup failures**.

questions.question: What does 'at' mean in a Java stack trace and how do you use it to find the bug?
questions.title: Reading the 'at' Lines in Stack Traces
questions.direct_answer: Each `at` line is a captured stack frame in the form `package.Class.method(File.java:line)` when source information is available. Frames are printed most-recent first. The top frame is often where the throwable was created or thrown, while a nearby application frame shows how owned code reached it. Native, unknown-source, omitted, and asynchronous frames need additional context.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- One `at` line equals one captured method frame
- Normal form is `Class.method(File.java:line)`
- Order is most recent call first, then older callers
- `Unknown Source`, native frames, and `... n more` have special meanings
- Async work may require traces or correlation beyond one thread's stack

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Each `at` line is one captured method frame. With source information it looks like `com.example.Calc.divide(Calc.java:12)`. Frames are ordered from the most recent captured call toward its callers, so the first frame often shows where the throwable was created or raised. If that frame is in a library, I scan toward the application caller to see which owned operation and inputs reached it. I treat the file and line as a pointer into the matching deployed source, not a guarantee that the fault is on that exact line. Generated code can show `Unknown Source`, native code can show `Native Method`, and nested causes abbreviate shared tails with `... n more`. Async or reactive work may cross thread boundaries, so one stack may need correlation logs or tracing to reconstruct the wider path.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
An `at` line represents one method on the captured call stack. A normal frame names the module or class, method, file, and source line, for example `com.example.OrderService.place(OrderService.java:42)`. Debug symbols or runtime-generated code may instead show `Unknown Source` or `Native Method`.

Frames are ordered from the most recent captured call toward its callers. The first frame often identifies where the throwable was constructed or raised. If that frame belongs to a library, scan toward the caller in application code to see what input or operation reached it.

`... n more` means shared tail frames were omitted from a nested cause, not that the trace lost all context. Async and reactive frameworks may add assembly traces or cross thread boundaries, so correlation IDs, thread dumps, or tracing may be needed beyond one synchronous stack.

sections.title: Anatomy of an 'at' Line
sections.content:
blue|package.Class|~Where|com.app.OrderService|which class|your code vs framework
emerald|.method|~What ran|the method executing|in that frame|the call
amber|(File.java:line)|~Exact spot|clickable in IDE|go here|the line number
rose|Order|~Newest first|top = throw point|down = callers|bottom = main

sections.title: Decoding 'at' Lines
sections.content:
```text
java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero
    at com.app.Calc.divide(Calc.java:12)   <- thrown HERE (top, your code)
    at com.app.Calc.run(Calc.java:6)        <- called divide()
    at com.app.Main.main(Main.java:4)       <- program entry (bottom)
```

Reads as: `divide` (Calc.java line 12) threw the exception; it was called by `run` (line 6), which was called by `main` (line 4). Open `Calc.java:12` first.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reading bottom-up**: the bottom is `main`, not the failure; the top `at` is the throw point.
- **Ignoring File.java:line**: it's a direct jump target — use it.
- **Skipping your own frames**: scan past framework `at` lines to the first one in your package.
